title: Prabowo’s partial multialignment is losing focus
gist: Probo Darono Yakti argues Prabowo's 'partial multialignment' (China and Australia 2+2s, Putin's Eastern Economic Forum, BRICS membership alongside OECD accession) is sound in principle but losing focus because Jakarta accumulates partners faster than it ranks their purposes. Relationships carry unequal weight, e.g. China's economic leverage and a US trade deal eliminating tariffs on 99% of US goods while keeping a 19% US tariff, so Indonesia needs a clear hierarchy of interests and non-negotiables.

insights.claim: In August Jakarta hosted the second Indonesia–China 2+2 dialogue and days later its tenth 2+2 with Australia; in September Prabowo was Putin's guest of honour at Vladivostok's Eastern Economic Forum, while Indonesia is a BRICS member pursuing OECD accession.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: Indonesia is hedging broadly, complicating bloc-based assumptions about its alignment.

insights.claim: Jakarta is accumulating relationships faster than it decides what each is for, so a strategy meant to widen room for manoeuvre ends up making choices harder.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: Policy unpredictability raises risk for investors betting on Indonesian alignment.
insights.quote: Jakarta is accumulating relationships faster than it is deciding what each relationship is for.

insights.claim: Calling Indonesia's course 'drift' treats inconsistency as the starting point rather than the outcome of uneven partnerships; engaging rival powers is not itself a strategic failure.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: Reframes Indonesia's mixed signals as manageable rather than directionless.

insights.claim: Partial multialignment is not equidistance: Indonesia can seek Chinese investment, Western markets and defence technology, and Russian cooperation simultaneously; BRICS membership does not require anti-Westernism.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: Indonesia remains open to Western capital despite BRICS membership.

insights.claim: China's economic importance gives Beijing influence over Indonesia that symbolic diversification cannot easily offset.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: China remains the dominant external economic lever on Indonesia.

insights.claim: The February 2026 US–Indonesia reciprocal trade agreement would eliminate tariffs on over 99% of US products entering Indonesia while keeping a 19% US reciprocal tariff on most Indonesian goods, with some exemptions.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: Asymmetric tariff terms favour US exporters and weigh on Indonesian export competitiveness.

insights.claim: Russia absorbs considerable presidential attention and defence cooperation interest but offers neither China's economic scale nor the West's market, technology and institutional access, so it does not balance constraints elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: Russia ties are diplomatic signalling more than economic substance.

insights.claim: Prabowo's highly presidential foreign policy gives speed but lacks coordination across trade, defence procurement, critical minerals and infrastructure, so a concession helping one ministry may constrain another.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: Critical minerals and infrastructure deals may carry hidden cross-sector commitments.
insights.quote: A concession that appears advantageous to one ministry may constrain another part of government later.

insights.claim: Major agreements should be tested on three questions: what concrete Indonesian interest is served, what dependency or expectation is created, and whether Jakarta can later reject it without a disproportionate price.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: A lens for judging durability of Indonesian deals with foreign partners.

insights.claim: Indonesia should set non-negotiables: sovereignty, control over critical infrastructure, freedom to choose defence suppliers and ability to maintain relations with competing powers.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: Signals potential limits on foreign control of Indonesian critical infrastructure.

insights.claim: Strategic autonomy is measured not by how many doors Jakarta can open but by whether it still decides which doors to close.
insights.speaker: Probo Darono Yakti
insights.so_what: Watch for Indonesia's willingness to refuse partner demands as an autonomy signal.
insights.quote: Strategic autonomy is not measured by how many doors Jakarta can open. It is measured by whether Jakarta still decides which doors to close.
